title: Capturing the Friedmans
full_review:
"Capturing the Friedmans" (Magnolia) is an unsettling documentary about a Long Island family torn apart by charges of pedophilia against the father and one son. It's not pretty, but, as with a roadside accident, your attention is riveted on the calamity.

It might have been an unremarkable film by Andrew Jarecki had he simply recounted the facts, the 1988 court proceedings and the outcome.

However, during his research, the eldest of the three Friedman sons, David, revealed they had copious videotape of their family life, including the bitter arguments after dad Arnold and youngest son Jesse were arrested and then released on bail.

Some of this footage, combined with contemporary interviews of family members, attorneys and law enforcement officers involved in the case, presents a head-twirling perspective on what happened, how it was handled, the community reaction and contradictory views of the truth.

What emerges about the Friedmans is generations of apparent sexual dysfunction, beginning with the promiscuity of Arnold's mother, witnessed by him as a little boy. Arnold's wife, Elaine, was shocked when a search warrant produced reams of child pornography in his den. And son Jesse's lawyer, Peter Panaro, reveals his client suffered molestation at the hands of his father -- although Jesse subsequently denied this.

David, currently Manhattan's leading birthday party clown, is the most volatile in the family, loudly protesting his father's innocence to this day and dismissing his mother as an idiot. His whining tirades are indicative of how deeply the criminal charges have affected more than just the accused as years later emotional wounds continue to fester.

Middle son Seth, now living in California, chose not to participate at all in the film and is seen only in the home movies.

And viewers are bound to wonder why the family was so obsessive about recording their lives, and not just the typical birthdays, holiday meals and vacations. There is David raging on his personal video diary; bland Arnold mugging and joking the night before he is incarcerated; Elaine defending herself against her sons' cruel insults; and Jesse bizarrely play-acting outside the courthouse just before his own sentencing. Between the family members in denial and contradictory perceptions, it is sad evidence of a familial breakdown.

Shaping this into a compelling documentary is editor Richard Hankin, who fluidly takes the audience back and forth from the 1980s to the present day to try to sort out what really happened. Award-winning high school teacher Arnold and his 18-year-old son Jesse were taken from their home the day before Thanksgiving 1987, eventually accused of sexually abusing young boys whom Arnold tutored at home in computer studies.

Questions about how law enforcement handled the case at the time arise when one of the victims suggests he was pressured by the police to claim abuse. Another remembered molestation only after hypnosis, raising questions about the issue of false memories, especially in the absence of any physical evidence.

Filmmaker Jarecki allows everyone his and her say from the distraught Friedmans to police officers, the judge, an investigative journalist, attorneys and Arnold's brother, Howard, who stands up for the now-deceased Arnold. The story never slumps as the viewer is continually called upon to size up who is credible and who seems to be altering the facts. Jarecki also manages not to demonize anyone while at the same time never making light of the serious and repellant nature of the crimes.

The result is a troubling, fascinating film that certainly points to the frailty of the human condition.

Due to sexual references, specifically pedophilia, and much rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
